key_insight: Channel geometry alone can substantially tune capillary-driven flow and analyte confinement in paper-based microdevices, with circular channels moving fastest and diverging-converging channels slowest.
engineering_relevance: Geometry-guided channel design offers a simple passive control strategy for low-cost paper microfluidics, enabling better transport timing and localized preconcentration without active pumping.
method: Fabricated five cellulose-paper channel geometries with equal area: converging-diverging, diverging-converging, wide-to-narrow, circular, and rectangular.
Tracked capillary transport using pyrene and benz[α]anthracene fluorescence under UV to quantify analyte confinement.
Used geometry-adapted Lucas–Washburn analysis plus CFD simulations calibrated to experiments and checked with mesh independence.
evidence_signal: Measured transport times ranged from 23.1 s for circular channels to 65.0 s for diverging-converging channels, with CFD and geometry-adapted Lucas–Washburn predictions showing semi-quantitative agreement with the observed velocity distributions.
watch_item: The reported confinement and flow behavior may depend on the specific paper substrate and cyclodextrin-functionalized chitosan coating, so direct transfer to other materials or analytes may require recalibration.
paper_title: Geometry-Driven Passive Fluid Transport in Paper-Based Microdevices
